paper-ca94ba207eb2244088e5: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems claim 2026 · doi 10.1145/3772318.3791517 · Route A 0 Identity and position work_id S2W-33CB81B366C5059542575B40 publication_form other contribution_types primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, design principle, framework or design space theory_position_tldr A six-week deployment of an LLM writing assistant in a real South Korean middle school, and one of the few papers in this corpus whose subject is a support failing. Van de Pol's six scaffolding strategies were written straight into the system prompt, with an explicit instruction not to give the answer at once, and 157 eighth-graders used the result across two writing units. The finding the review needs is the split between what happened under the tool and what survived it. In class the sentences built with the assistant were grammatically sound for everyone, most of all for the weakest students at 86.2%. Two to three weeks later, writing the same essay with no teacher and no AI, high performers carried 65.8% of those sentences correctly into their own work and low performers 14.0%. Alongside that, frustration ran roughly three times higher in the lower groups and piled up in the second half of each period, because a hint-only design costs time a student in a 45-minute lesson does not control. The authors therefore argue against the field's own non-disclosure norm. The classroom effects are as consequential: four or five students of 26 kept the teacher's attention, quiet students asked less than before, peer questions went to the machine, and the recurring questions the teacher used to diagnose the room stopped arriving. No control condition, groups cut from the outcome score itself, and correctness judged by GPT-4o. overall_uncertainty medium · The core comparison is unusually well placed: the same sentences are scored under the tool and, two to three weeks later, in an essay written with no teacher and no AI. That the transfer gap runs 65.8, 37.8 and 14.0 down the proficiency scale while in-class accuracy did not is hard to explain away. What weakens the size of every group number is the same three things. There is no control condition and no pre-test, so nothing compares these students against no tool or a direct-answer tool. The performance groups are cut from the score on the very assessment the transfer is measured in, which is circular. And grammatical correctness was judged by GPT-4o on the strength of one cited preprint. The qualitative and classroom findings rest on fifteen coded students, three observed sessions and one teacher who also co-designed the system; students were never asked anything, by design. Directions are solid, magnitudes are not. 1 8 page-grounded claims Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page. Claim 1 · CLAIM-001 effect, failure, condition The paper's most useful result, and the reason it belongs in this review: the support did not fail while it was present, it failed on removal, and it failed hardest for the students it was built for. Under the tool the low-performing group's sentences were the most grammatically accurate of any group, 86.2%. Two to three weeks later, writing the same-topic essay alone with no teacher and no AI, that group carried 14.0% of those sentences correctly into their own work, against 37.8% for the middle group and 65.8% for the high group. An in-class artifact gap of nothing became a post-removal gap of nearly five to one. Two things bound the claim and neither is small. What is measured is whether an LLM-built sentence reappeared correctly in the later essay, which is reuse, not knowledge: a student who wrote something different or better scores as a non-transfer, and the paper does not separate those cases. And the groups are defined by the score on that same later assessment, so the split is partly circular. The denominators behind 65.8, 37.8 and 14.0 are not printed, the analysis covers one semester and one feature, and grammatical correctness was judged by GPT-4o rather than a person. author_claim_text During the fall semester, students constructed a total of 632 sentences with the assistance of an LLM. Of these, 309 sentences (48.9% of the total) were incorporated verbatim into the students' final essays, with 82.3% of them being grammatically correct. This trend was also observed in the low-performing group, where 86.2% of the sentences constructed with the LLM were grammatically accurate. However, while students in the high-performing group correctly incorporated 65.8% of these sentences into their final written assessments, students in the middle- and low-performing groups only did so 37.8% and 14.0% of the time, respectively. These findings suggest that, regardless of proficiency level, the use of an LLM can serve as an effective tool for improving students' grammatical accuracy during in-class activities. (PDF p. 1) Abstract — The headline as the authors state it: a deployment with 157 eighth-graders in a South Korean middle school English class over six weeks, in which scaffolding improved students' ability to compose grammatically correct sentences while the step-by-step approach demotivated lower-proficiency students and increased their system reliance. (PDF p. 12) 8 Conclusion — The conclusion in the authors' own summary: LLMs improved grammatical accuracy and offered scalable assistance, the step-by-step scaffolding sometimes hindered lower-proficiency students under time constraints and contributed to demotivation and over-reliance, introverted students asked fewer questions, peer learning declined, struggling students' difficulties were masked by AI-polished outputs, and taken together the support can unintentionally widen proficiency gaps. reviewer inference (PDF p. 9) 5.2 RQ2 — This is the most valuable number in the paper and the one the review most needs. Held under the tool, the low-performing group's LLM-built sentences were the most grammatically accurate of any group at 86.2%; asked to write the same essay alone two to three weeks later, that group carried only 14.0% of those sentences correctly into their own work, against 65.8% for the high group. What is measured is whether an LLM-built sentence reappeared correctly, not whether grammar was learned, so a student who wrote something better of their own counts as a non-transfer. And the group split is small: 632 sentences, one semester, one feature, with the per-group denominators not printed. (PDF p. 5) 4.4 Written Assessment — The grouping is circular in a way that matters for every per-group number on this card. High, middle and low are defined by the score on the post-removal written assessment, and that same assessment is the artifact the transfer rate is measured in. So a student who reproduced few LLM sentences is more likely to have scored low, and being low is what puts them in the low group. That does not make the gradient false, it makes its size unreliable, and it means none of these groups is an independent measure of English proficiency taken before the tool arrived. (PDF p. 6) 4.5 Analysis — The measurement chain deserves stating plainly, because three of the paper's headline numbers pass through it. paper-4c33b0debd374ee62b2f: Revisiting the Hint Button: Consistent Negative Associations Between Unproductive Hint Use and Learning Outcomes in Intelligent Tutoring Systems Proceedings of the LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference claim 2026 · doi 10.1145/3785022.3785040 · Route A 0 Identity and position work_id S2W-F687971C80F0A48660F80F54 publication_form other contribution_types primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method, design principle theory_position_tldr Three semesters of log data from a K-12 decimals game built on an intelligent tutoring system, 999 students of 1,370, asking what on-demand hints actually do. The system works on average: pretest 22.17 of 52 points, immediate posttest 24.88, one-week delayed posttest 25.30, a large pre-to-post effect. The average hides everything, because the standard deviation of the gain, 6.39 points, is more than twice the mean gain of 2.71. Two behaviours computed from ordinary logs explain part of the spread and both point the same way. Asking for a hint before making any attempt, and clicking past hints faster than the words could be read at four words a second, each correlate negatively with the pretest, the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest in all three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each stays a significant negative predictor after prior knowledge is controlled. The students who do it most are the ones with the least prior knowledge, so the authors conclude that freely available hints may widen rather than close the gap. Their explanation is about the interface, not the learner: a persistent hint button is an affordance for bypass, and for a student who clicks straight to the bottom-out hint the tutor is effectively a screen that displays the answer before the problem starts. It is correlational, from observational data, and the authors say so. overall_uncertainty medium · The strongest evidence in this corpus for help degrading the learning it was built to support, and it is still correlational. What it has: 999 students across three cohorts and 4 to 6 schools per semester, counterbalanced test versions, a one-week delayed posttest taken away from the system, indicators computed from complete interaction logs, and eighteen coefficients that all point the same way at p < .001. What it does not have: any manipulation of hint availability, so the causal direction is open and the authors state that plainly. The obvious confound is prior knowledge, and controlling for the pretest does not remove the association but does not exclude a third factor such as disengagement either. Two further gaps matter. The abstract says the associations are particularly pronounced among lower-knowledge learners, and no interaction or subgroup model is reported; only the frequency of the behaviour is shown to differ by quartile. And the cohorts are described as the three semesters with hint access, implying no-hint semesters that are never compared. Carry the replicated negative associations and the affordance argument; do not carry a causal effect of hints. 1 6 page-grounded claims Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page. Claim 1 · CLAIM-001 effect, failure The most direct evidence in this corpus that help can be consumed in a way that predicts worse capability once the help is gone, and it is measured that way: the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest are paper tests taken in class, away from the tutor, so every coefficient describes unsupported performance. Two behaviours read off ordinary logs, asking before attempting and clicking past hints faster than they can be read, correlate negatively with the pretest, the immediate posttest and the delayed posttest in each of three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each remains a significant negative predictor once the pretest is controlled. Eighteen coefficients, all negative, all at p < .001, across 999 students and up to six schools a semester. What it is not is a demonstration that hints caused the damage. Nothing was manipulated; a student who leans on hints and a student who learns little may simply be the same student, and one prior-knowledge covariate does not exclude that. The defensible carry is that heavy, shallow help use marks a trajectory towards poor unsupported performance, and that it is cheap to detect. author_claim_text Through a multi-semester analysis of 999 K–12 mathematics students, this study demonstrates that simple, interpretable indicators of unproductive hint use—premature hint requests and superficial hint reading—are consistently associated with reduced learning gains across cohorts. These associations persist after controlling for prior knowledge... This behavior effectively degrades the hint system from a scaffold for learning into a shortcut to answers, undermining its intended pedagogical benefits. serves Earlier outline · Work process (now RQ2) · Earlier outline · Cognition and learning (now RQ2) · Earlier chapter · Conditional outcomes · S2Q3 · Limits and unanswered evidence applies_to a digital learning game with an underlying intelligent tutoring system, played in regular class time, with tests administered separately on paper; 999 K-12 mathematics students of 1,370 who participated, across three semesters and 4 to 6 schools each; on-demand three-level hints reached by a persistent hint button, ending in a bottom-out hint that states the answer; The relationships are correlational and from observational data, and the authors say they do not establish causation. It is one of the very few systems in this corpus that instructs its support to recede: the appendix tells the model to provide support and gradually withdraw it, to help the user perform the task on their own, and not to provide a full solution. The behavioural result is the strongest thing here and it is measured on the right side of the conversation. Against the baseline, the model generated solutions 32 times instead of 243, users wrote 178 words per turn instead of 67 while the model wrote fewer, sessions ran twice as many turns, and the share of user utterances that answered a question from the system rose twelvefold. So the work moved from the machine to the person, which is what the design intended. What is not shown is anything about the person afterwards. Both sessions lasted ten minutes, every outcome is a process trace or a perception rating, and whether the model actually faded within a session is never checked. overall_uncertainty medium · The process measurements are good and unusually well suited to this review: 24 practitioners, within-subject, counterbalanced order, transcripts coded against two named schemes with Cohen's kappa of 0.79 on 50% double-coded logs, and the counts reported separately for mentor-driven and mentee-driven behaviours so the reader can see who did the work. The limits are equally clear. Each condition ran ten minutes on the participant's own artifact, so the comparison is between two brief conversations rather than between two ways of learning. Every outcome is either a conversational trace or a Likert perception, several of the reported differences are not significant and are described as comparably better anyway, and the qualitative claims rest on a handful of participants. Most importantly for this card, the system's central instruction — provide support and gradually withdraw it — is never verified: no analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session, and no measurement is taken after the session at all. Claim 1 · CLAIM-001 principle, mechanism This is what withdrawal looks like when the support is a language model, and it deserves recording precisely because it is so unlike everything else in the corpus. The mechanism is a sentence in a system prompt: provide your support and gradually withdraw it, help them perform tasks on their own, do not provide a full solution. There is no schedule, no diagnostic, no representation of what this user can now do, and no threshold at which anything changes. The fading is delegated wholesale to the model's reading of the conversation in front of it. Set against the argumentation review's finding that the only fading anyone builds is a fixed timetable, and that the timetable does worse than never fading, this is a genuinely different move: support that could in principle recede when this particular person stops needing it, because the thing deciding is reading what they just said. Whether it does is not established. No analysis tests whether support declined across the turns of a session; the evidence offered is that annotators labelled 26 turns as scaffolding against none in the baseline, which counts occurrences and not a trajectory. Publication counts are rising and fields are mixing; survey papers answer this where they exist and go stale where they do not; search engines find papers but leave the connections between them to the reader, which is cited as the step nobody supports; and the graph and cluster tools that try to show those connections are faulted with a specific finding, that automatic clusters conflate several dimensions at once and readers cannot work out what a cluster means. Against that sits the observation the whole system rests on, cited to two sources, that authors already summarise and connect prior work in their related work sections, and that each such paragraph carries context and structure around the papers it names. paper-148cd9b36b0f41346f31: Analyzing human–computer interaction as distributed cognition: The resources model Human-Computer Interaction claim 2000 · doi 10.1207/s15327051hci1501_01 · Route A 0 Identity and position work_id S2W-C2BC1C535DC36FA581F31E3E publication_form other contribution_types concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, lineage or history theory_position_tldr The founding attempt to turn distributed cognition into something an interface analyst can use. Wright, Fields and Harrison argue that distributed cognition makes external resources for action central but never defines them well enough to analyse anything, so they supply the definition: six abstract information structures a support can carry, which are plans, goals, possibilities, history, action-effect relations and states, each able to sit in the head, in the artifact, or be split; and four ways of deciding what to do next, each with a stated list of which structures it requires. Three things are worth carrying. That strategy-to-resource table is a design space in one page, saying which ways of working a configuration of support permits and which it forecloses. The co-location principle is concrete and reusable: coordination gets cheap when the resources a strategy must bring together sit in the same external space, which is why a speed bug beside the airspeed needle turns arithmetic into looking. And the Chart Wizard analysis names a failure mode in the authors' own words: a plan externalised one dialogue box at a time drives the interaction rather than resourcing it, confounding control structure with information resource, so the user can neither see the plan nor work another way. What the paper does not contain is evidence. The authors say outright that they do not aim to validate the model empirically and that the right validation is uptake by designers. Their one study, an 8 puzzle from an unpublished MSc thesis, is reported with no sample size, measure or statistic. And across 82,477 folded characters the words scaffolding, fading, withdrawal, contingency, dependence and over-reliance appear zero times. overall_uncertainty high · High as a source of vocabulary and design distinctions, near zero as a source of evidence, and the paper says so itself. It is a 37-page theory article in a top journal, and its conceptual work is careful: the six structures and four strategies are defined, the abstract-versus-representation distinction is held consistently, and a cockpit checklist, a spreadsheet wizard and a sliding tile puzzle are each worked through in detail. But the authors state in the introduction that they do not aim to validate the model by testing its predictions, and in the conclusion that validation means uptake by designers. Every empirical statement is either a summary of someone else's study or a forward reference to work reported elsewhere. The one study claimed as their own, the 8 puzzle variations, is an unpublished MSc thesis by a student of the first author, reported with no sample size, task measure, move count or test; the sentence claiming stronger evidence than a prior published study has nothing printed behind it. The Chart Wizard walkthrough is one analyst's prediction about one hypothetical user, never tested. Read it for what it defines; treat every claim about people as untested. 1 6 page-grounded claims Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page. Claim 1 · CLAIM-001 concept or lineage, principle This is a design space for external support stated as a vocabulary plus a requirements table, and it is the most directly reusable thing in the paper. Six structures name what a support can carry: the plan, the goal, the set of currently possible actions, the history of what has been done, the mapping from action to effect, and the current state. Each may sit in the person's head, in the artifact, or be split between them. Four strategies name ways of working, and Figure 2 says which structures each one requires, so a configuration of support can be read off against which ways of working it enables and which it forecloses. Withhold history and history-based choice becomes unavailable; withhold action-effect information and both goal matching and plan construction lose an input they need. That turns a vague question about how much help to give into a specific question about which structures a design externalises, and it applies to any support for structured work rather than only to graphical interfaces.
